Name: Thulani Dhlamini

linearity: Yes, I often feel restricted by the linear nature of BI tools like Power BI. The workflow expects me to apply one filter or transformation at a time, and once I move forward, there’s no structured way to keep track of the rationale behind earlier steps. For example, if I filter destinations by safety and then add affordability, the "why" behind my sequence gets buried in the report state. This makes it difficult to capture my initial hypotheses (e.g., "safety might matter more than cost") because the tool only reflects the current applied filters, not the thought process. The result is a fragile exploration path where reasoning and experimentation can easily get lost.
branching: The biggest barrier was that Power BI doesn’t support parallel branches natively. To compare "affordability-first" versus "safety-first," I had to create duplicate pages or rely on bookmarks. Both are clunky: bookmarks break easily when visuals or slicers change, and duplicate pages make it hard to keep filters synchronized. As a workaround, I often resort to taking screenshots and pasting them into OneNote or PowerPoint so I can view branches side by side. This external workaround costs extra time and introduces the risk of working with stale or inconsistent snapshots instead of live, connected data.
reflection: Revisiting earlier steps is challenging because the BI workflow doesn’t preserve a reasoning history. If I decide that crowd dynamics are more important than affordability, I have to manually adjust parameters and filters from scratch. There’s no "version history" of my exploration where I can easily roll back or tweak earlier decisions while preserving the rest of my work. I end up re-applying slicers, recalculating measures, or rebuilding visuals, which is inefficient. Often, I have to write down parameter values or copy screenshots externally so I don’t lose track of what I tested before.
explainability: It would be hard to defend the evolution of my reasoning, why I shifted weights, why certain branches were discarded, and how trade-offs were considered. The BI tool shows the final state (e.g., top 3 destinations based on active filters) but not the alternative paths I explored along the way. If a stakeholder asked, "Why did you prioritize safety over affordability?" I would have to dig through notes or screenshots rather than pointing to an integrated history in the tool. Similarly, explaining parameter adjustments (like raising the weight of crowd avoidance after reflection) is difficult because there’s no built-in record of those changes. This makes my final narrative less transparent and harder to justify fully within the tool itself.
B-2: Without a clear question, the tool does not provide much guidance. I often have to create my own starting point by dragging in fields, building exploratory visuals, or applying slicers manually. There’s no dedicated space to capture vague goals or hypotheses, so it’s easy to feel lost or unfocused. I usually rely on external notes to shape my direction before the BI workflow feels useful.
B-4: The tool shows my final state (e.g., top 3 destinations by score), but it doesn’t capture the reasoning steps, parameter changes, or alternative branches I explored. To build a narrative, I take screenshots, export CSVs, or add text boxes manually, then piece these together in PowerPoint or notes. It’s possible to reach a structured recommendation, but it requires significant extra effort outside the tool.
B-10: The tool makes it relatively simple to try a new chart type, adjust slicers, or change parameters, so in that sense it does encourage experimenting. However, because each change overwrites the previous view, I often lose context or have to duplicate pages/bookmarks to preserve earlier trials. This makes branching less natural, so while it’s possible to try different analyses, it doesn’t feel seamless or strongly encouraged.
B-12: It is quite hard to track multiple exploration paths inside the tool. I usually rely on bookmarks or duplicate reports, but those break easily and don’t show changes in reasoning over time. To truly keep track, I end up exporting screenshots or notes outside the tool. Without a built-in "exploration history" or side-by-side comparison feature, it requires significant manual effort to maintain parallel paths.
B-14: The tool does not explicitly show the sequence of my reasoning or the earlier parameter choices I made. I can usually sense when I need to revisit a step (e.g., realizing that crowd dynamics matter more than affordability), but actually recognizing where in the workflow to go back is harder because prior decisions are buried in filters or overwritten by new visuals. Without a history log, I rely on external notes to remind myself of earlier assumptions.
B-16: The tool allows me to adjust weights and create comparisons, but it doesn’t naturally support keeping multiple trade-off scenarios visible at once. As a result, while I can reflect on trade-offs, the tool itself doesn’t make that process very easy or natural.
B-18: The tool can show the final visuals, metrics, and rankings clearly, but it does not capture the evolution of my reasoning or the alternative paths I explored.
